At the best tip-speed ratio the wind's torque is proportional to v2, and so to Ω2; a square law with the right k balances it at λ∗ in every wind, so the rotor settles at its best speed by itself. Below 8.98 rpm the law has a kink: there the torque ramps down in a straight line to zero at 6.9 rpm, so that the turbine starts and stops gently. At a steady 8 m/s the two torques balance at 9.07 rpm, 1.0 % below the λ∗v/rrot​ of section 0.3, because that ramp holds the rotor a little off its best ratio.

A gusty wind. Turbines are designed against a standard description of gusty wind, set out in the international standard IEC 61400-1. Its strongest class of turbulence, class A, makes the wind's speed at 8 m/s fluctuate with a standard deviation of 1.86 m/s, 23 % of the mean. How that fluctuation spreads over slow and fast changes is given by the Kaimal spectrum, a formula fitted to measured winds: most of it lies in changes lasting tens of seconds to minutes, and less and less in quicker wiggles. Two points of the rotor's disc a few tens of metres apart wander together only in the slow changes, so the wind averaged over the disc, which is what turns the rotor, is smoother than the wind at any one point. NREL's program TurbSim generates such winds; these notes use 40 generated ten-minute records at a mean of 8 m/s, not measurements. In them the rotor's speed wanders about its mean with a standard deviation of 10.3 % of the mean. Only 8 m/s was simulated.

What the second blade feels. The gusts reach the second blade in two ways. While the rotor speeds up or slows down, the Euler torque of (1.5) acts; it changes the power by about 2 parts in 10 000, nothing. More important, the rotor's speed itself changes. The second blade settles to a new speed in about a second (section 3.1), while the rotor's speed changes over tens of seconds, so at every moment the second blade swings as it would at that moment's speed in a steady wind. With the hinge generator's constant c fixed, (2.3) at the speed Ω, divided by its value at the speed Ω0​ for which c is the best brake, is

Pˉ(Ω0​)Pˉ(Ω)​=1+Ω2/Ω02​2​.

(In rotor turns, R stays the same at every speed, but κ=c/(IΩ) and G change with Ω; this formula carries both.) Its slope at Ω0​ is −1: a shift of the mean speed by a fraction ϵ changes the power by −ϵ. And it curves upwards there (its second derivative in Ω/Ω0​ is +1), so a speed that wanders about a fixed mean raises the average power, whichever way it wanders: by about s2/2 for a relative spread s, 0.53 % here.

On our blade
The full equation of the second blade was run through each of the 40 records, with the rotor's speed taken from the turbine's own equation, and compared with steady rotation. Two main-generator rules were tried. With a pure square law (Qgen​∝Ω2, no kink) the second blade's power changes by +0.77 % against steady operation at 8 m/s: the wandering speed adds +0.90 %, a little more than the 0.53 % the curvature alone predicts (we have not traced the rest), and the mean speed moves by +0.11 % and changes the power by −0.11 %, as the slope of −1 predicts. With the turbine's real torque law, kink included, the total turns to −1.99 %. At 8 m/s the rotor runs just above the kink. In a lull it drops onto the ramp, where the main generator brakes much less, so it slows less than it speeds up in a gust; its mean speed rises by +2.60 %, which changes the power by −2.55 %, again as the slope predicts, while the wander still adds +0.53 %. That is a property of this turbine's control, not of the wind. Either way, gusts change the second blade's power by a few per cent.
What to remember
  • The rotor is a flywheel: gusts make its speed wander slowly, by about a tenth.
  • The second blade follows the rotor's speed from moment to moment. A wander about a fixed mean adds a little; a shift of the mean speed by a fraction ϵ costs ϵ of the power.
  • Net effect at 8 m/s: a few per cent, its sign set by the main generator's torque law.

6 The blade bends and shakes

A real blade is not rigid. It bends under its own weight, once per turn, and it shakes in gusty wind near its own edgewise frequency. Both move the hinge, and at the tip they move it most.

6.1 The sag: a large push that cancels itself

Hold a long, springy ruler out sideways and turn your wrist slowly: the ruler sags first one way and then the other, following gravity, and its end sags most. A blade 61.5 m long does the same as it turns, in its own plane.

The blade's mass and stiffness, metre by metre, are published (the OpenFAST blade file of the 5 MW turbine). From them, gravity bends the blade edgewise so that its tip moves to and fro by w = 431 to 467 mm either side of its straight position, once per turn and in step with gravity's push; the range comes from two ways of taking the shape of the bend, from the blade's first mode of vibration or by integrating the bending directly. The hinge, at the tip, therefore moves across the mother blade by wcosφ.

That motion adds to gravity's push in two ways, each worth Ω2w per kilogram. First, seen from the turning mother blade, the hinge accelerates to and fro by −Ω2wcosφ, which in the hinge's frame is an apparent push of +Ω2wcosφ, in step with gravity's. Second, a hinge moved sideways by wcosφ sits at a slightly different angle seen from the hub, wcosφ/rp​, so the outward pull, which points away from the hub, turns by that angle, and its part across the mother blade grows by Ω2rp​⋅wcosφ/rp​=Ω2wcosφ. Together, gravity's push g becomes g+2Ω2w. (Linearising the Lagrangian with a moving hinge, in SymPy, gives the same.) On its own that would raise the power, which goes as the push squared (2.5), by 16.9 to 18.4 % at 8 m/s.

But a bending blade also turns: each cross-section tilts with the slope of the bend, and at the tip the slope is largest. The generator's stator, fixed in the mother blade, tilts with it by an angle β. The generator brakes the second blade's motion relative to the stator, −c(θ˙−β˙​), so the tilting stator drags the second blade with the extra torque cβ˙​. That drag follows the rate of change of the slope, a quarter turn out of step with the sag's push, while at the best brake the swing lags its push by 45° (section 2.3); so part of the drag works against the swing. The two effects largely cancel. What is left is a small difference of two large numbers, so it depends on the exact shape of the bend: a net change of +2.2 to +3.5 % for the two shapes. (For the first shape, linear theory and a full nonlinear run with the moving, tilting hinge agree within 0.2 percentage points.) The lesson: a generator brakes motion relative to its own frame, so when that frame moves, the frame's motion counts too.

6.2 Random shaking

Gusts make the blade's first edgewise mode vibrate near 1.08 Hz. How far the tip of this blade vibrates edgewise in ordinary operation, we found no published value. So the notes take a range of tip vibrations, 5, 20 and 100 mm rms, and say what each would give; the answer rests on that unknown.

The model has two parts, coupled both ways. The blade's first edgewise mode is one oscillator: a modal mass, the mass that, sitting at the tip on a spring, would vibrate like the whole blade in that mode (1416 kg, computed from the blade's mass table and the mode's shape), on a spring tuned to 1.08 Hz, with a damping ratio ζb​ of 0.5 % or 3 % of critical, two assumed values. It is driven by a random force whose spectrum is flat near 1.08 Hz, scaled so that the blade alone would vibrate at the stated tip level. At the tip the hinge moves sideways with the tip, and the section tilts by 28.1 mrad per metre of tip motion. The second blade is (2.1) with its hinge shaken sideways and its stator tilted by that much, and it pushes back on the blade's mode with the force and torque it needs. Gravity's push is left out of this part (it is in chapter 2 and section 6.1). Everything is linear, so the response is computed frequency by frequency, and the generator's mean power is the brake times the mean square of the relative speed. (The full linear equations, with the second blade integrated along its length and the turning frame's centrifugal and Coriolis terms, were derived in SymPy.) The model checks that the second blade never takes more than the gusts feed into the blade.

On our blade
At a 5 mm tip vibration the gusts feed 0.110 W into the blade's vibration, and the 1 m second blade, at its best brake for the shaking, 1.89 N m s, takes 3.38 mW of it. At 20 mm it takes 54.2 mW; at 100 mm, 1 350 mW, more than gravity gives. For comparison, gravity gives 202 mW at its own best brake, 29.6 N m s. Since the model is linear, the swings from shaking and from gravity add; but the two best brakes differ by a factor of fifteen, so the two best powers cannot simply be added. At the shaking's best brake the second blade's damping ratio is only 0.3: here, unlike under gravity's push, it really does ring. The motion is regular (section 3.4).

The 1 m second blade takes so little at small vibrations because its own frequency, R​ times the rotor's, is 1.36 times the blade's: it is far from the blade's resonance. A second blade tuned to the blade, its own frequency Ω3rp​/(2l)​ equal to the blade's ωe​=2π×1.08 Hz at the mean rotor speed, needs a length of 1.85 m; with the same mass per metre it weighs 1.85 kg. It would then be a tuned mass damper, the device that calms swaying skyscrapers, and it would draw on the blade's vibration directly: at 5 mm and 0.5 % blade damping, the linear model gives it 64.6 mW. But gravity's term −Gθsinφ (section 2.1) stiffens and softens it once per turn, shifting its frequency by ±1/(2Γ)=±8.6 % at 8 m/s, while the blade's resonance is only 1 to 6 % wide; the rotor's wandering speed detunes it too. So it is detuned and retuned every turn, and whether any of that gain survives is an open question that only a calculation in time, with gravity kept whole, can answer.

What to remember
  • The blade's sag moves and tilts the hinge once per turn. The two effects largely cancel: a few per cent net.
  • A generator brakes motion relative to its own frame; when the frame moves, that counts.
  • The blade's random vibration adds power as the square of the tip's vibration: negligible at 5 mm, more than gravity at 100 mm. The real level for this blade is not known, so this stays open.

7 From swing to watts

Every chapter so far has treated the generator as a perfect brake: a torque −cθ˙ that takes the power cθ˙2 and loses none of it. A real one is a small electric motor driven backwards, behind a gearbox. This chapter takes one from a catalogue, puts it in the hinge, follows the power from the swinging second blade to the wires of the sensor, and then sizes the second blade to suit it.

7.1 A generator is a brake

A bicycle dynamo pressed against the tyre makes the wheel harder to turn when the lamp is lit, and harder still if you join its two wires together; with the wires loose it spins almost freely. What pushes back on the wheel is the electric current.

A small motor with permanent magnets has two constants. Turning its shaft at the angular speed ωm​ induces the voltage e=ke​ωm​ in its coil, by Faraday's law; this voltage is called the back-EMF (electromotive force), because in a motor it pushes back against the supply. A current i in the coil gives a torque kt​i on the shaft. The two constants are equal in SI units, because the electrical power ei and the mechanical power kt​iωm​ are the same power. Connect a load resistor RL​: the current is i=e/(Rc​+RL​), where Rc​ is the resistance of the coil itself. The torque on the shaft is then kt​ke​ωm​/(Rc​+RL​), proportional to the speed: exactly the brake of chapter 1. (The coil's inductance would delay the current by Lc​/Rc​=0.12 ms, nothing next to a swing that lasts seconds, and is left out.)

Between the second blade and the motor sits a gearbox of ratio N: the motor turns N times for each turn of the hinge, ωm​=Nθ˙, and its torque reaches the second blade multiplied by N. The ratio therefore enters twice, once in the voltage and once in the torque, and the brake constant at the hinge is

ce​=Rc​+RL​N2kt​ke​​.
(7.1)

The power ce​θ˙2 is the electrical power ei, and the current shares it between the coil and the load in proportion to their resistances. The load gets the fraction RL​/(Rc​+RL​). Call csc​=N2kt​ke​/Rc​ the brake with the wires joined (RL​=0, the "short circuit"): it is the strongest brake this motor can give through this gearbox. Since RL​/(Rc​+RL​)=1−ce​/csc​,

Pload​=ce​(1−csc​ce​​)⟨θ˙2⟩.
(7.2)

This is section 2.3's contest once more, now inside the generator: a brake near the short circuit takes plenty of power but burns it in its own coil; a light brake sends nearly all of it to the load but takes little.

On our blade
Take the maxon RE 25, a motor 25 mm across, rated 20 W, in its 24 V winding: Rc​=1.53 Ω, kt​=20.8 mN m/A, and a speed constant of 460 rpm/V, which is ke​=60/(2π⋅460)=0.02076 V s; the two constants agree to the catalogue's rounding, two parts in a thousand. Without a gearbox its strongest brake is csc​=kt​ke​/Rc​=0.000282 N m s. The best brake of chapter 2, (2.6), is 22.4 to 37.4 N m s: some 79 000 to 130 000 times more. Because the brake grows as N2, a ratio of at least 282 to 364 is needed just to reach the best brake with the wires joined. The reason is the shape of the job. At the best brake the second blade pushes with 3.47 N m (section 2.3) while its hinge turns at only 0.09 to 0.15 rad/s at its fastest; a small motor is built to give a hundredth of that torque (the RE 25's rated torque is 30.4 mN m) at thousands of rpm. The gearbox converts one into the other.

7.2 What the gearbox costs

Turn the crank of a hand-held egg beater. The beaters are light, yet the crank feels heavy when you start and stop it, because each turn of the crank spins the beaters four times. Seen from the slow side, everything on the fast side of a gearbox is magnified: a torque by N, and an inertia by N2.

The gearbox that makes the brake strong enough brings three costs.

Inertia. The motor's rotor, of moment of inertia J, turns at Nθ˙, so its kinetic energy is 21​JN2θ˙2: to the second blade it is an extra moment of inertia JN2 about the hinge. In the units of chapter 1, where the second blade's own is I, it adds

j=IJN2​.
(7.3)

It does not feel the centrifugal pull or gravity, because the motor's rotor sits on the hinge's axis; it only resists being accelerated. In (2.2) the second blade's inertia gave the −1 of the net stiffness R−1; the rotor adds its own, and the net stiffness becomes R−1−j.

Friction. Brushes and bearings resist turning with a torque T0​ that hardly depends on speed. Through the gearbox it reaches the second blade as NT0​.

Gear losses. A gearhead's efficiency η is the fraction of the power it passes on, whichever way the power flows. While the second blade drives the motor, every torque the motor side needs costs the second blade N/η times that torque, not N times; while the motor's spinning rotor slows down and gives its energy back, the second blade receives only η of it. In the formula below we keep the simple part: the brake the second blade feels is ce​/η and the friction NT0​/η, and the rotor's inertia passes without loss. The full equation of section 7.4 charges the loss on every flow.

Put the three into (1.6): the rotor's inertia joins θ′′, the brake becomes κe​/η, and the friction is a torque of constant size f that always opposes the swing:

(1+j)θ′′+ηκe​​θ′+fsgnθ′+Rsinθ+Gcos(φ+θ)=0,κe​=IΩce​​,f=ηIΩ2NT0​​.
(7.4)

In these units gravity's largest torque, 2ml​g, is G, so f/G=NT0​/(η2ml​g) compares the friction with the push that drives the swing, and it is the same at every wind. If f≥G the friction is stronger than gravity can ever push, and a second blade at rest never moves: the gearbox has jammed it.

On our blade
The RE 25's rotor has J=14.7 g cm², and the GP 32 C gearhead adds 0.7 to 1.5 g cm² at its input. (A planetary gearhead is a compact gearbox in which small gear wheels, the planets, run round a central one, the sun, inside a ring; several such stages in a row multiply their ratios.) Through the largest catalogue ratio, 492 : 1, that gives j=1.12: against a net stiffness R−1=93.5, nothing. The catalogue gives no friction torque; the no-load current, 40.2 mA, gives an estimate T0​≈kt​i0​=0.84 mN m, measured at 10 900 rpm. The gearhead's catalogue efficiency is 80 % for one stage, 75 % for two, 70 % for three and 60 % for four. Through 492 : 1 (four stages) the friction at the hinge is 0.686 N m, 14 % of gravity's largest torque 2ml​g=4.90 N m. At the catalogue's friction the second blade would jam only beyond a ratio of 4 105 on a three-stage gearhead and 3 518 on a four-stage one: no catalogue ratio jams it.

Two of these numbers are less certain than the rest. The catalogue gives the gearhead's best forward efficiency, driven from the motor at its best load; driven backwards and lightly loaded, a gearhead can do worse. And friction measured at 10 900 rpm includes losses that grow with speed, so at the slow speeds here it may be lower. The first makes the numbers below optimistic, the second pessimistic. Only a test on a bench can settle them.

7.3 Friction as a brake that weakens

Push a heavy box across the floor. The floor pushes back with the same force whether you walk or run, so it takes the same toll for every metre. A brake like the dynamo is different: it pushes back harder the faster you go.

Equation (7.4) is no longer linear, because of sgnθ′, but chapter 2's method still works with one more step. Suppose the second blade still swings as θ=−Θcos(φ−δ). The friction torque fsgnθ′ is then a square wave, +f while the blade moves one way and −f while it moves back, in step with θ′. A square wave of height f is a sum of sine waves at frequencies 1, 3, 5, …, the first of amplitude 4f/π and the others of 1/3, 1/5, … of it. Keep only the first, the one at the frequency of the swing. A damper κf​θ′ gives a torque of amplitude κf​Θ in step with θ′, so the friction acts like a damper with

κf​=πΘ4f​.
(7.5)

This is called the describing function of friction. It is a brake that weakens as the swing grows, since the toll per swing is fixed but the swing is longer. In (2.2), replace R−1 by R−1−j and κ by κe​/η+κf​, and multiply through by Θ:

Θ2(R−1−j)2+(ηκe​​Θ+π4f​)2=G2.
(7.6)

This is a quadratic equation for Θ. It has a positive root only if 4f/π<G, a slightly stricter form of the jamming condition above. The power the load receives is (7.2) with ⟨θ˙2⟩=Ω2Θ2/2, and the rotor pays for everything the second blade loses, in the coil, the load, the gears and the friction:

Pload​=IΩ3κe​(1−csc​ce​​)2Θ2​,Protor​=IΩ3[ηκe​​2Θ2​+π2​fΘ].
(7.7)

The last term is the friction's toll: torque times the mean speed ⟨∣θ′∣⟩=2Θ/π.

Check
Remove the losses: f=0, j=0, η=1 and csc​→∞ (a coil without resistance). Then (7.6) is (2.2), and both powers in (7.7) become (2.3). Units: κe​, j, f and G are pure numbers, and IΩ3 is a power.

7.4 On our blade

Formulas (7.6) and (7.7) give, at each wind and each catalogue ratio of the GP 32 C, the load resistor that gives the load the most power, with the peak torque at the hinge within the torque the gearhead may carry continuously (6 N m for the largest ratios) and the swing below 0.5 rad, the range in which these notes use the formula (the best settings swing at most 0.22 rad, so that limit never bites); ratios that jam are out. Then, as a second route, the full equation is solved with the method of section 3.1. It is (7.4) with the gear loss charged on every power that flows through the gearhead. Let x be the torque the motor side needs, as felt through a perfect gear (in the units of (7.4), and without η in the friction: f0​=NT0​/(IΩ2)); the second blade feels x/η while power flows into the motor side and ηx while it flows back:

θ′′+Rsinθ+Gcos(φ+θ)+kx=0,x=jθ′′+f0​sgnθ′+κe​θ′,k=η−sgn(xθ′).
(7.8)

Because θ′′ appears on both sides, each step solves for it (the left side grows steadily with θ′′, so there is exactly one answer). Each sign is smoothed over a narrow band: a thousandth of the swing for sgnθ′, and a thousandth of the gear's own power scale for sgn(xθ′). The full equation is run at the formula's brake and at half and twice it, at every wind, and at 8 m/s with every other ratio at its own best brake; the rotor's work is integrated too, so the energy book closes in the full equation as well.

On our blade

The load receives 57 to 106 mW: 36 to 40 % of what the perfect brake of chapter 2 would take, and 35 to 39 % of what the rotor pays. The motor's friction takes 14 to 15 % of what the rotor pays; the gears and the coil take most of the rest. The largest ratio, 492, wins at every wind: a smaller one cannot brake hard enough without burning most of the power in the coil. Even so the motor brakes only 0.39 to 0.43 of the best brake (2.6), which is why the second blade swings wider than in chapter 2 and gives less. Even the strongest wind, which gives the least, gives more than 1 500 times what the minimal sensor of section 0.5 needs. The full equation agrees with the formula within 2.1 %, and of the three brakes tried, the formula's is the best.

Follow the power down the chain, from the rotor to the load: of what the rotor pays, the motor's friction takes 14 to 15 %, the gears and the coil's resistance most of the rest, and 35 to 39 % reaches the load.

How much do the two uncertain numbers of section 7.2 matter? By the formula: if the gearhead's own drag doubles the friction, the load gets 41 to 75 mW; if the backdriven efficiency is 50 % instead of the catalogue's 60 %, 46 to 84 mW; with both, 30 to 57 mW, still 811 times the sensor's need.

One more thing the sensor's designer must know: the voltage. The load sees an alternating voltage that peaks at 0.80 to 1.39 V and alternates once per turn, at 0.114 to 0.191 Hz, with the motor turning at most 743 rpm, far below the gearhead's limit of 8000 rpm. Turning that into the steady few volts a radio chip needs is a problem of electronics that these notes do not solve. The motor's graphite brushes also have a voltage drop of their own where they touch the turning commutator; the catalogue does not give it, and at peaks of about a volt it could matter, so it too waits for a bench test. The margins above are therefore before the electronics, and a bench test of the whole chain is the next step.

7.5 Sizing the second blade to its generator

Chapter 2 says the power grows with the second blade's first moment, and (2.6) says the best brake grows with it too: c∗≈2ml​rp​Ω. A given generator can brake only so hard, so for a given generator there is a second blade it serves best. Too light a second blade asks for a brake the motor gives easily, but takes little; too heavy a one asks for more brake than the motor can give, or more torque than its gearhead may carry, and the motor takes only a small share of what the second blade could give.

On our blade

With twice the catalogue's friction and a gear efficiency of 50 %, the 1 kg second blade still gives the sensor 811 times its need at the poorest wind.

7.6 Bigger second blades

Hang a ruler and a plank side by side from the rim of a turning wheel. Both lean back by the same few degrees, because gravity's push and the outward pull both grow with how much mass sits how far from the hinge. But to hold the plank against its swing you need a far stronger hand than for the ruler.

Our second blade is light for a blade tip. The NREL blade itself weighs 10.3 kg per metre at its very tip, and its outer 3 m weigh 115 kg. Real devices fitted at blade tips are of the same build: retrofit tip extensions reach about one metre past the old tip and are about three metres long in all (a Vestas patent, US 10 927 809, listed with the sources below), and the tip brakes of older turbines (section 0.5), on turbines that limit their power in strong wind by letting their blades stall rather than by turning them, are 5 to 20 % of the rotor radius long (US patent 8 403 641, also below). So it is worth asking what the formulas of chapters 2 and 7 give over that range. Table 5 runs them for lengths from half a metre to three metres and for four mass densities: a light hollow sensor blade (1 kg per metre), a light composite (3 kg per metre), the mother blade's own tip (10 kg per metre) and its build a metre further in (30 kg per metre).

Three things follow. First, the best power grows in proportion to the first moment ml/2, as (2.7) says: at 6 m/s from 66.7 mW to 74.0 W over the table. Second, the swing does not change: Θ∗ at 6 m/s stays between 0.214 and 0.220 rad for every size. The reason is in (2.2): at the best brake Θ∗=G/[2​(R−1)], and gravity's push G and the centrifugal stiffness R both carry the same factor 2ml​/I, so their ratio is g/(Ω2rp​) for any second blade much shorter than its mother blade, which gives 0.213 rad. Third, the torque the generator must hold, τ∗, grows with the first moment too, from 0.867 to 936 N m. The RE 25 behind its gearhead cannot follow: once the first moment passes about half a kilogram-metre, it delivers 93.9 to 107 mW at 6 m/s whatever the size, because the gearhead's continuous torque, not the second blade, sets the limit. A bigger second blade needs a bigger generator, sized by τ∗ and c∗ as in section 7.5. The largest blades of the table also pull on the mother blade's tip with up to 8.34 kN at 10 m/s, close to the pull of its own outer 3 m, 10.1 kN; such a device would need a check of the blade's structure, which these notes do not make. Ours adds 91 N.

For the minimal sensor, every size in the table is more than enough: through the RE 25 the poorest case, the smallest blade in the strongest wind, still gives 311 times its need. So the size is not set by that sensor. These notes size the second blade for the most power from one small catalogue generator, because a sensor that does more can use it (section 0.5): 1 kg on 1 m is the lightest second blade that generator serves fully, and the lightest load on the mother blade's tip.

What to remember
  • A motor driven backwards is a brake: ce​=N2kt​ke​/(Rc​+RL​). The load gets the share RL​/(Rc​+RL​) of what it brakes, so a stronger brake and a larger share pull against each other.
  • A gearbox turns a small, fast motor into a strong, slow brake. It costs inertia (negligible here), friction (a brake that weakens as the swing grows) and gear losses.
  • Through a catalogue motor and gearhead the load receives 57 to 106 mW, 35 to 39 % of what the rotor pays.
  • Bigger second blades give proportionally more, but need a generator that holds a proportionally larger torque.
Problems
  1. Without a gearbox, the RE 25's strongest brake is 0.000282 N m s. What gear ratio does it need, at the least, to reach the best brake of 6 and of 10 m/s?
    AnswerThe brake grows as N2, so N≥c∗/csc​​: 282 at 6 m/s and 364 at 10 m/s. And that is with the wires joined, when the coil burns everything; a load needs a still larger ratio.
  2. With the wires joined (RL​=0), how much power reaches the load? And with the wires apart (RL​→∞)?
    AnswerNone either way. Joined, the brake is strongest but all its power heats the coil; apart, no current flows and the motor does not brake at all. In between lies a best load, the contest of section 2.3 once more.
  3. The motor's friction proved ten times the catalogue's estimate. Would the four-stage gearhead at 492 : 1 jam the second blade?
    AnswerAt the catalogue's friction it jams only beyond a ratio of 3 518; the jamming ratio falls in proportion to the friction, so ten times the friction jams it beyond about a tenth of that, below 492. Yes, it would jam: the friction would hold the second blade still against gravity's push. A bench test of the friction comes first.
  4. How fast does the motor turn at most, through 492 : 1, and why is that slow for a motor?
    AnswerAt most 743 rpm, at 6 m/s, where the swing is fastest. Small motors are built for thousands of rpm; here even a 492-fold gearbox leaves it turning slowly, which is why its voltage peaks at only about a volt.

8 The answer

8.1 The ceiling

Lower a bag of shopping on a rope: the power you can take from it is its weight times the speed at which it falls, however it falls. The second blade is the same, with its weight acting at its centre of mass, l/2 from the hinge, and moving relative to the mother blade at the speed 2l​∣θ˙∣.

The mechanics of these notes meets in one inequality. Watch the second blade from the turning mother blade, with the rotor's speed steady and the mother blade rigid. In this frame gravity does the work; seen from the ground, the same energy comes from the rotor (section 1.8). The two are one bookkeeping in two frames. There the centrifugal pull is a fixed field of force with a potential energy, so over a steady turn it gives as much as it takes; the Coriolis force is always at right angles to the motion and does no work. Gravity is the only force whose direction changes, and the only one that can feed the swing on average. Its torque on the second blade is −2ml​gcos(φ+θ), never larger than 2ml​g, so the power it feeds in, and with it every watt the generator can take, obeys

Pˉ≤2ml​g⟨∣θ˙∣⟩.
(8.1)

It holds for any motion: small swings or large, regular or chaotic, with any brake and any gearbox. (A rotor whose speed wanders, or a blade that shakes, adds a feed of its own: a few per cent from gusts and sag, and from the blade's vibration an amount that depends on a vibration level we could not find (chapters 5 and 6). The air, left out of these notes, would add a feed of its own too.) To harvest more, the second blade must move faster, and a stiff centrifugal spring does not let it. At the best brake of chapter 2 the power is P∗=21​τ∗ΩΘ∗ with τ∗=2ml​g/2​, a fixed fraction, π/(42​)=0.555, of the right side of (8.1): the best brake already takes more than half of what gravity could ever give at that swing.

The inequality also names the one design lever that always works: the right side grows with the first moment 2ml​. A heavier second blade, or one whose mass sits farther out, gives proportionally more, as (2.7) says. What limits it is the generator, whose best brake (2.6) and torque τ∗ grow with the first moment too (section 7.5), and the air.

8.2 What the second blade can and cannot do

The question was how much power a second blade hinged at the tip of a turbine blade can give, who pays for it, and what the wind's gusts and the blade's motion add. The answers, in short:

  • A uniform second blade of 1 kg and 1 m takes 161 to 267 mW from the rotor at steady winds of 10 to 6 m/s, by the best-brake rule κ∗=R−1, and the rotor pays for every joule. The power grows with the first moment ml/2 and falls with the speed of the hinge, so it is largest in light wind (chapters 2 and 3).
  • Resonance is out of reach for any second blade shorter than its mother blade, and the motion is regular at every wind and brake tried (chapters 2 and 3).
  • Gusts change the power by a few per cent (chapter 5), and so does the mother blade's sag under its own weight (chapter 6). Random shaking of white-noise type can feed in at most 2S​ times three quarters of the second blade's mass, whatever the motion (chapter 4). The blade's real vibration is the open question: the second blade takes little from tip vibrations of 5 mm and more than gravity gives at 100 mm, and we found no published value for this blade (chapter 6).
  • A real geared generator from a catalogue delivers 57 to 106 mW to the load, more than 1 500 times what the minimal sensor of section 0.5 needs, and still hundreds of times if the gearbox proves twice as draggy and less efficient than its catalogue (chapter 7). The second blade is sized to that generator. Turning its slow alternating voltage into a steady supply is an open problem of electronics.

What the mechanics leaves open is the air. At the tip the second blade moves through the air at 45.3 to 75.5 m/s, and section 0.7 showed that a few square centimetres of it, at a force coefficient of one, would feel a force as large as its weight. A real second blade, many times larger, would be pushed by the air at least as hard as by gravity. That push could feed the swing, as a flag's flutter is fed by the wind, or damp it; it would certainly load the hinge and the generator. These notes answer the question for the mechanics alone: gravity, turning once per revolution as seen from the blade, drives a swing worth about a fifth of a watt for a kilogram on a metre, and the rotor pays for it without noticing. The air must be modelled before these numbers can be trusted for a real tip device; it is the next model, and it decides whether this machine is worth building.
